content:
Soundcheck began with a broken cable and Greg lying flat on the stage as if the floor had betrayed him. The boardwalk stage before the town fundraiser had its own weather, noises, and opinion about whether I was prepared. I stood in the middle of it with the kind of courage that appears after a person has already said yes. The reflex to run had not vanished because love became possible. It had simply lost the argument for the morning.

The plan was to help Greg prepare without turning his nervousness into another problem. Greg wrote it on a receipt, then copied it onto cleaner paper when he decided the first version looked too much like a confession. Nothing was complicated, which made it frightening. Complicated plans came with exits. This one asked us to notice what we were building while we were building it. I kept my hands busy with stage dust, warm strings, and the hush before an audience listens and tried not to count the ways a good day could become a test.

Greg arrived with one joke already spent and another held in reserve. He was good at making a room less sharp. He was also good at hiding the bruise beneath the joke if nobody asked him to stop. He tuned by ear, apologized to the microphone, and looked toward me between every song. When he looked at me, the familiar warmth was there, along with the question he was trying not to ask: was I staying because I wanted him, or because I had grown used to being wanted?

I answered by taking an active part in the mess. I took the second guitar and told him I would follow his tempo only if he stopped pretending he did not want me there. It mattered to do something that could not be mistaken for passive trust. Greg made space for people so generously that they could forget he needed space too. I did not want to accept his care as an endless resource. I wanted to meet him in the middle, where a hand could be offered and still be allowed to pull back.

The complication was already there: the organizer wanted polished music while Greg wanted to play what had actually kept him alive. It was not a disaster. Beach City produced problems small enough to laugh at and serious enough to reveal a person. Greg's shoulders tightened. His instinct was to fix the practical thing first, then ask whether anyone had feelings about it. I caught his wrist before he disappeared into the task. He looked down at my hand as if I had interrupted a song.

“You can fix it,” I said. “You do not have to fix it this second.”

Greg considered this. “That is a deeply unfair distinction.”

“It is also useful.”

“Useful is how trouble gets invited into the house.”

“Trouble already has a key.”

That made him laugh without letting him off the hook. He sat beside me. The space between our knees was narrow and warm. For a few breaths, he let the world remain imperfect while he listened to me breathe. I loved that about him: not that he always knew what to say, but that he could learn to stay after the first answer failed.

We talked about the first unfinished chord he played when we met. The object was ordinary when it entered our lives, but ordinary things collected meaning when we returned to them. Greg told the story again, leaving out the version where he made himself the fool. He had been young, lonely, and brave in ways he did not know how to name. I was not interested in punishing the person he had been. I was interested in the person beside me now, still learning how to ask.

“A song does not need to be perfect to tell the truth.” Greg said, embarrassed by the wisdom of his own sentence.

“You rehearsed that.”

“I rehearsed three worse versions.”

“Are they available?”

“Only in the director's cut.”

His grin softened when I touched his face. The gesture was not a reward. It was an answer to the question beneath the joke. He leaned into my palm, broad and warm and real. The ache in him did not make him fragile. It made his tenderness deliberate. He knew what it cost to lose a life, and he still chose to build another.

By late afternoon, the practical work became a rhythm. I handed him tools. He handed me decisions. We argued about small things and discovered that disagreement did not have to become abandonment. The sharp edge of the problem eased when neither of us tried to win. When the room quieted, Greg rested his forehead against mine. “I am proud of you,” he said. The praise went through me more cleanly than I expected. I had treated praise like a trapdoor. Greg offered it like a chair.

We took a break without calling it one. Greg found something cold to drink, and I sat where I could see the work waiting for us without being swallowed by it. He told me three small stories about stage dust, warm strings, and the hush before an audience listens: one funny, one embarrassing, and one that ended with him admitting he had been scared. I answered with a truth of my own. The exchange was not dramatic enough for a song, which was exactly why it mattered. Real intimacy kept happening in the unlit spaces between declarations. I could be tired and still be wanted. Greg could be uncertain and still be someone I trusted. We did not have to turn every feeling into a performance before it counted.

When we went back to the task, I noticed how often Greg checked my face. Each glance was quick enough to pretend it was practical, but I knew the question now. I answered it by staying engaged: moving closer, asking for the tool I needed, and telling him when I wanted a pause. He listened without turning my boundaries into a punishment. That kind of listening made room for desire rather than shrinking it. By the time we had a solution to the problem, we had also made a quieter discovery: the two of us could build a day that had room for work, laughter, fear, and wanting without making any one of them apologize for taking up space.

I wrote one sentence on the clean side of Greg's receipt: I am here because I choose to be. He read it, then folded the paper carefully and tucked it into his pocket. “For the record,” he said, “I am keeping this.” I told him he was allowed to keep the sentence as long as he did not use it as evidence in an argument. He promised to weaponize it only for sentimental purposes. The promise was ridiculous. It was also sincere.

For a little while, we simply kept each other company. The ordinary quiet had its own kind of courage. I did not need to impress him, and he did not need to turn himself into a story worth telling. We were two adults making room for one another in a day that had started with a plan and ended with something more useful: proof that closeness could be chosen repeatedly, in small motions, without either of us losing a self we had worked hard to become.

I told him what I wanted next. Someone called him a novelty act and the old shame still had teeth. Greg did not rush to reassure me. He did not promise never to fail or never to need more than I could give. He promised to tell me when fear was driving. That was better. A perfect man would have been a stranger. Greg was a person with a van, a guitar, a history of running, and a stubborn desire to come home honestly.

When we touched, it was with the care of people who understood that wanting could be generous. I fixed the collar of his shirt behind the curtain and let him kiss me first. The moment stayed specific to us: his awkward laugh, my hand in his hair, and the way he asked whether I was comfortable and believed me when I answered. Nothing had to become explicit to become intense. The door could close. The story could trust us with what happened on the other side.

Afterward, Greg brought water. I stole the blanket. He complained that it had always preferred him, and I told him it was responding to character development. The joke landed softly. So did the silence afterward. We had crossed another threshold. The world had not changed shape, but the relationship had. Someone called him a novelty act and the old shame still had teeth no longer sounded like a problem we had to solve before happiness was allowed.

At the end of the day, the next thing became clear: He handed me the set list with my name beside the last song. Greg's shoulder pressed against mine as the light moved across the room. The future arrived as a thing we could touch: a key, a song, a repaired hinge, a cup left on the counter for the person who would wake later. I let myself believe in the next morning without demanding that it guarantee every morning after. For now, that was enough.
